title: Maintenance treatment with capecitabine and bevacizumab in metastatic colorectal cancer (CAIRO3): a phase 3 randomised controlled trial of the Dutch Colorectal Cancer Group.
passage: Curated paraphrase of the independently inspected abstract: This open-label phase 3 trial randomized 558 adults with previously untreated metastatic colorectal cancer, WHO performance status 0 or 1, adequate organ function, and stable disease or better after six three-weekly cycles of capecitabine, oxaliplatin and bevacizumab. Maintenance capecitabine plus bevacizumab was compared with observation; reintroduction of CAPOX-bevacizumab was planned at first progression. Median time from randomization to second progression, the primary endpoint PFS2, was 11.7 months with maintenance versus 8.5 months with observation, with a hazard ratio of 0.67 and 95% confidence interval 0.56 to 0.81. Global quality of life did not deteriorate during maintenance and was not clinically different between groups. Hand-foot skin reaction occurred in 64 patients, 23%, during maintenance. These findings concern a maintenance-and-reintroduction strategy, not selection for conversion surgery.
limitations: The original article abstract was inspected through the Europe PMC API; publisher full text, protocol and supplements were not reviewed.
The eligible population had disease control after six cycles of CAPOX-bevacizumab. Applicability is limited when induction drugs, duration, performance status or treatment intent differ.
The primary endpoint was PFS2 measured from randomization, not overall survival or cure. No overall-survival benefit is asserted from this abstract.
The trial does not establish an indication, deadline or mandate for conversion surgery and does not validate an individual perioperative treatment plan.
The record date is the independent source access and review date, not the publication date. This is curated evidence, not a live runtime internet lookup.

title: Prospective Dutch colorectal cancer cohort: an infrastructure for long-term observational, prognostic, predictive and (randomized) intervention research.
passage: Curated paraphrase of the independently inspected abstract: The Prospective Dutch Colorectal Cancer cohort is described as a nationwide, multidisciplinary, prospective observational infrastructure open to patients with stage I to IV colorectal cancer. It collects longitudinal clinical information from routine practice, with separate consent for blood and tumor tissue collection, patient questionnaires and broad randomization for embedded cohort multiple randomized controlled trials. The objectives are long-term clinical, patient-reported outcome and biomaterial collection, and facilitation of future basic, translational, interventional and cost-effectiveness research. The publication describes an infrastructure and its early implementation; it does not demonstrate randomized treatment benefit or establish present-day recruitment availability.
limitations: The original 2016 publication was reviewed at complete indexed-abstract level only; its full protocol and consent documentation were not inspected.
This is an observational cohort infrastructure publication, not a randomized comparison demonstrating that a specific treatment improves outcomes.
Separate embedded randomized studies require their own eligibility, intervention, outcome and source verification.
Historical enrollment statements in the publication do not establish active enrollment, a participating local site, patient eligibility or consent on 2026-09-17.
Broad stage I to IV coverage does not establish the representativeness or adequacy of a particular molecular, metastatic or perioperative subgroup.
The record date is the independent source access and review date, not the publication date. This is curated evidence, not a live runtime internet lookup.

title: Proactive vs Reactive Treatment of Hypotension During Surgery: The PRETREAT Randomized Clinical Trial.
passage: Curated paraphrase of the independently inspected abstract and accessible methods: PRETREAT compared proactive intraoperative blood-pressure management stratified by predicted hypotension risk with usual care in adults undergoing elective noncardiac surgery at two Dutch tertiary hospitals. The intervention assigned mean arterial pressure targets of at least 70, 80 or 90 mm Hg to low-, intermediate- or high-risk groups; these were study targets, not prescriptions for an individual patient. The primary outcome was functional disability six months after surgery using the 12-item WHODAS 2.0 scale. The trial stopped early for futility. In the 3247-patient population described in the abstract, six-month mean disability scores were 17.7 with proactive management and 18.2 with usual care, a mean difference of -0.5 with a 95% credible interval from -1.9 to 0.9. The abstract reports no significant differences in any of 23 secondary outcomes. The study did not establish improved long-term disability from this risk-stratified strategy.
limitations: The complete indexed abstract and publicly accessible methods were inspected, but a complete original-article results and discussion review was not achieved. The record is conservatively classified as abstract-only.

The study population comprised elective noncardiac surgical patients, not an exclusively major-abdominal-surgery or colorectal-cancer population. Individual or procedure-specific benefit is not established.

The accessible methods specify adults receiving general or central-neuraxial anesthesia with an expected postoperative stay of at least one night; low-risk surgery, obstetric procedures and organ transplantation were among exclusions.
The trial stopped early for futility. Its neutral clinical results do not prove that all blood-pressure strategies or all higher-risk subgroups are equivalent.
A physiological or clinician-behavior effect must not be presented as proof of improved disability, complications or survival.
The numerical blood-pressure targets describe the experimental strategy only and must not be generalized into an individualized blood-pressure or medication prescription.
The record date is the independent source access and review date, not the publication date. This is curated evidence, not a live runtime internet lookup.

title: Impact of risk assessments on prophylactic antiemetic prescription and the incidence of postoperative nausea and vomiting: a cluster-randomized trial.
passage: Curated paraphrase of the independently inspected abstract: In this single-center cluster-randomized trial, anesthesiologists were allocated to receive or not receive automated postoperative nausea and vomiting risk calculations without patient-specific prophylactic antiemetic recommendations. The analysis included 11613 elective surgical patients treated by 57 anesthesiologists after exclusion of small clinician clusters. Risk display increased prophylactic antiemetic administration and risk-tailoring, but did not establish a reduction in postoperative nausea and vomiting within 24 hours. Crude incidences were 41% with risk display and 43% with care as usual; the reported odds ratio was 0.97 with a 95% confidence interval of 0.87 to 1.1. The antiemetic administration rate ratio was 2.0 with a 95% confidence interval of 1.6 to 2.4. Changes in prescribing behavior therefore did not establish improved patient outcomes in this implementation.
limitations: Only the complete indexed abstract was inspected. Full methods, risk-model specification, protocol and supplementary analyses were not reviewed.
This was a single-center implementation study with clinician-level randomization; clinician clusters treating fewer than 50 enrolled patients were excluded from analysis.
The intervention displayed predicted risk without patient-specific therapeutic recommendations; it should not be conflated with the subsequent directive intervention.
The study involved elective surgical patients generally, not a verified major-abdominal-surgery subgroup.
The crude two-percentage-point incidence difference is not proof of benefit; the reported effect estimate did not establish a reduction in the primary outcome.
The results do not prescribe an individual patient's prophylactic regimen or imply that all risk-display systems are ineffective.
The record date is the independent source access and review date, not the publication date. This is curated evidence, not a live runtime internet lookup.

title: Impact of adding therapeutic recommendations to risk assessments from a prediction model for postoperative nausea and vomiting.
passage: Curated paraphrase of the independently inspected abstract: This separate prospective before-after study included 1483 elective surgical inpatients. It compared a care-as-usual period with a subsequent period using predicted postoperative nausea and vomiting risk together with specific therapeutic recommendations. During the directive-intervention period, clinicians administered 0.5 more prophylactic antiemetics to patients identified as being at greater risk, with a 95% confidence interval of 0.4 to 0.6. The reported odds ratio for postoperative nausea and vomiting was 0.60, with a 95% confidence interval of 0.43 to 0.83; the high-risk estimate was 0.45, with a 95% confidence interval of 0.28 to 0.72. These findings describe an association between directive implementation and improved outcomes in a nonrandomized before-after comparison. The contrast with the earlier assistive risk-display trial was across separate studies, not a randomized head-to-head comparison of directive and assistive support.
limitations: Only the complete indexed abstract was inspected; publisher full-text access was blocked. Detailed intervention thresholds, outcome ascertainment and follow-up timing were not independently extracted.
This was a prospective before-after study, not a randomized trial and not merely a secondary analysis of the earlier cluster-randomized trial.
Temporal change, case mix and other concurrent practice changes may confound a before-after comparison; the design cannot establish the same causal certainty as randomized allocation.
The study does not provide a randomized head-to-head estimate of directive versus assistive decision support.
The population was elective surgical inpatients generally; applicability to a particular major abdominal procedure or patient-specific risk profile remains partial.
The odds ratios must not be presented as absolute risk reductions, risk ratios or individualized benefit estimates.
The record date is the independent source access and review date, not the publication date. This is curated evidence, not a live runtime internet lookup.

title: First-line systemic treatment strategies in patients with initially unresectable colorectal cancer liver metastases (CAIRO5): an open-label, multicentre, randomised, controlled, phase 3 study from the Dutch Colorectal Cancer Group.
passage: Curated paraphrase of the independently inspected original 2023 abstract: CAIRO5 enrolled adults with initially unresectable colorectal cancer liver metastases, known RAS/BRAF V600E status and WHO performance status 0 or 1. A central expert panel assessed resectability at baseline and every two months using predefined criteria. Patients with left-sided, RAS and BRAF V600E wild-type tumors were randomized to FOLFOX or FOLFIRI plus bevacizumab, group C, or FOLFOX or FOLFIRI plus panitumumab, group D. These two groups closed prematurely for futility. In the modified intention-to-treat population, median progression-free survival was 10.8 months with bevacizumab versus 10.4 months with panitumumab; the reported stratified hazard ratio was 1.11 with a 95% confidence interval of 0.84 to 1.48 and p=0.46. Grade 3 to 4 skin toxicity and diarrhea were more frequent with panitumumab. This comparison informs induction-treatment evidence in the left-sided wild-type setting, but does not establish an optimal number of cycles before surgery or an individual indication or date for local treatment.
limitations: The complete original 2023 indexed abstract was inspected; the full article, protocol, supplements and predefined resectability criteria were not independently reviewed.
The relevant wild-type comparison requires both a left-sided primary and RAS/BRAF V600E wild-type status. RAS/BRAF wild-type status alone does not establish applicability to groups C and D.

The population had initially unresectable liver metastases and WHO performance status 0 or 1. Individual anatomy, extrahepatic findings, treatment tolerance and current resectability require separate review.
Groups C and D closed early for futility. Failure to demonstrate superiority is not proof that the treatments are equivalent.
Results from groups A and B, which enrolled right-sided or RAS/BRAF V600E-mutated disease, must not be substituted for the left-sided wild-type comparison.
The original abstract does not quantify complete local-treatment rates or establish an overall-survival advantage for the wild-type comparison; those outcomes are not asserted here.
Expert-panel reassessment every two months was a trial procedure, not evidence of optimal surgery timing or an individualized scheduling prescription.
This is an additional-case-specific projection of the canonical CRC-CAIRO5 publication record; it must not overwrite the original scenario's case-specific evidence.
The record date is the independent source access and review date, not the publication date. This is curated evidence, not a live runtime internet lookup.
